chapterTitle: ES6 Refresher: Essential JavaScript for React Native
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute interactive code-along video. Start with a basic JavaScript file (not React Native yet, just pure JS) to demonstrate `var`, `let`, `const` with examples of scope and reassignment. Then, introduce arrow functions with examples of implicit return and lexical `this` (perhaps in a simple `setTimeout` context). Move to destructuring objects and arrays, showing practical use cases. screens.title: ES6 Refresher: Essential JavaScript for React Native
screens.narratorSegment: Before we build interfaces in React Native, we need a reliable command of modern JavaScript. This lesson refreshes the core ES6 features you will use: block-scoped declarations, arrow functions, destructuring, the spread and rest operators, and ES6 modules. Each of these features reduces boilerplate and makes component code easier to reason about. For example, choosing a block-scoped declaration prevents accidental leakage of variables across loops and conditionals. Arrow functions keep your callbacks concise and avoid common mistakes with the this keyword in component methods. Destructuring and the spread operator let you pick only the values you need and produce immutable-looking updates without mutating originals. Finally, import and export let you organize logic into small, testable files used across screens and components. We will walk through practical examples, a guided refactor of a small component, and a short assessment that asks you to apply destructuring and rest. By the end you will know not just the syntax but the practical trade-offs and common pitfalls to avoid. Ready to make your JavaScript cleaner and safer for React Native?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will have clearly defined, demonstrable skills you can apply to React Native. First, you will differentiate var, let, and const, and explain block scope versus function scope with concrete examples that show why let and const are safer. Second, you will write arrow functions that use implicit return and understand lexical this, particularly when writing callbacks or handlers inside components. Third, you will destructure objects and arrays to extract values succinctly from props and A P I responses. Finally, you will combine spread and rest operators to copy, merge, and collect values without mutating originals. For each objective we pair a short practice mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can test yourself. These objectives are intentionally practical: you will refactor a small component to use const and arrow functions, apply destructuring to props, and use spread to merge styles. That work makes these objectives concrete, not abstract. As you study, look for how each feature reduces boilerplate and prevents specific bugs like accidental global variables, lost this context, or unintended object mutation.

screens.title: var, let, and const — scope and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the three main declaration keywords and compare their behavior with concrete examples. The older keyword is var, which is function-scoped and hoisted: a variable declared with var is visible throughout its containing function even before the declaration line runs. That behavior can lead to surprising bugs when variables appear to exist earlier than you expect. In contrast, let and const are block-scoped: their visibility is limited to the nearest pair of curly braces. That prevents accidental access from outside loops, conditionals, or nested blocks. The practical difference between let and const is reassignment. Use const for bindings that should not be reassigned; use let only when you need to update a variable. A common misconception is thinking const means an immutable object; actually it prevents reassigning the binding, but object properties or array elements can still be modified. For example, a constant array can have items pushed into it, but you cannot assign a new array to the same name. A good rule of thumb is to default to const and switch to let when you deliberately plan to reassign. This habit reduces accidental reassignments and clarifies intent in component code.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › var, let, const
Definition & Behavior
var is function-scoped and hoisted; let and const are block-scoped. const prevents reassigning a binding but does not freeze object contents.
Quick examples
// var is hoisted
console.log(message); // undefined
var message = 'hello';

// let and const are block-scoped
if (true) {
  let x = 1;
  const y = 2;
}
// x and y are not available here

// const with objects: contents can change
const arr = [1, 2];
arr.push(3); // OK
// arr = [4]; // Error: cannot reassign
Key takeaway
Default to const. Use let for reassignments and avoid var in new code.
Common mistake
Assuming const makes deep objects immutable; it only prevents reassigning the variable name.
Practical scenario
In a component loop, using let for the iterator prevents callbacks from capturing a single shared variable caused by var's function scope.
Example analogy
Think of block scope as a room: variables declared with let or const stay inside the room. var behaves like a building-level variable that every room can access, creating accidental collisions.
Try this
Refactor a small loop from var to let and confirm each callback captures the correct value.

screens.title: Using const effectively and mutability nuance
screens.narratorSegment: A small but important habit improves code safety: default to const. When you declare most variables with const, you communicate intent and reduce accidental reassignments. That habit makes refactors clearer because a later reader knows the binding is not meant to change. However, a common confusion is that const makes values immutable. In JavaScript, const prevents the name from being rebound to a new value, but if the value is an object or array its contents remain changeable. That means you can push into a constant array or set properties on a constant object. This distinction matters in React Native where state updates often require creating a new array or object rather than mutating an existing one. Use the spread operator to build new arrays or objects for state updates so you maintain immutable update patterns. In practice, prefer const for every binding that doesn't need reassignment, and be explicit about when you mutate an object — or better, avoid mutation and return a new copy. This approach reduces subtle bugs and makes your components easier to test. Using const effectively and mutability nuance means const signals intent not immutability. use spread patterns for state updates to avoid in-place mutation despite const bindings.. In practical terms, why default to const and how object mutation works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › const & mutability
Why default to const
Choosing const communicates that a binding should not change, making code easier to reason about during refactors.
// const prevents reassignment
const user = { name: 'Jo' };
user.name = 'Joanna'; // allowed: modifying contents
// user = { name: 'Other' } // Error: cannot reassign

// For immutable-style updates use spread
const newUser = { ...user, name: 'Joanna' };
Key takeaway
Use spread to create new objects/arrays when updating state, even if the original binding is const.
Practical example
In component state updates, avoid methods that mutate arrays in place. Instead, build a new array with the spread operator and pass it to setState or the state setter hook.
Common mistake
Mutating a constant object and relying on the reference to trigger updates. React detects reference changes, so a mutated object with the same reference may not re-render as expected.
Try replacing an in-place push on an array with a new array formed by spread and check that your component updates predictably.

screens.title: Arrow Functions and lexical this
screens.narratorSegment: Arrow functions simplify function expressions and clarify how this behaves inside callbacks. They provide concise syntax: a single-expression arrow implicitly returns that value, eliminating the return keyword. More importantly, arrow functions do not create their own this binding. Instead they inherit the this value from the enclosing lexical context. This trait addresses common pitfalls when passing callbacks to event handlers or timers inside components. For example, if you use a traditional function for a timer callback inside a component method, the this inside that callback may not refer to the component instance unless you explicitly bind it. Arrow functions capture the surrounding this, preventing that need. A common misconception is that arrow functions are always interchangeable with regular functions; they are not, because they cannot be used as constructors and they lack their own prototype. When you need a function with its own this or a constructor, use a normal function. For typical React Native callbacks and render helpers, arrow functions are concise and reliable. Arrow Functions and lexical this means use arrow functions for inline callbacks and handlers to inherit the surrounding this and avoid manual binding.. In practical terms, concise syntax and predictable this binding for callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use arrow functions for inline callbacks and handlers to inherit the surrounding this and avoid manual binding.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Arrow Functions
Syntax & Implicit return
A single-expression arrow returns that expression implicitly. Use parentheses for multiple parameters and braces for a function body that needs statements.
// implicit return
const add = (a, b) => a + b;

// body with statements
const logPlus = (a, b) => {
  const sum = a + b;
  console.log(sum);
  return sum;
};
Tip
Prefer implicit return for short expressions to keep callbacks concise in render code.
Lexical this example
Compare how this behaves in a timer callback when using a normal function vs an arrow function.
// Traditional function loses lexical this
function Timer(){
  this.count = 0;
  setTimeout(function(){
    // this here is not the Timer instance
    // so this.count is undefined
  }, 1000);
}

// Arrow function captures surrounding this
function TimerCorrect(){
  this.count = 0;
  setTimeout(() => {
    this.count += 1; // works as expected
  }, 1000);
}
Misconception
Arrow functions are not a drop-in replacement for methods that require their own this or for constructors.

screens.title: Destructuring objects — extract props with clarity
screens.narratorSegment: Destructuring extracts properties from objects into local variables in a concise form. This is especially useful in React Native for pulling props from a component's props object or fields from A P I responses. Instead of assigning each property one by one, destructuring lets you declare the variables you need in a single pattern. You can also rename properties or provide default values when a property might be absent. A common use case is extracting name and email from a user object returned by an A P I, which reduces repetition and improves readability. Another helpful pattern is nested destructuring for objects that contain nested shapes, but use it sparingly when nested depths grow deep as it can hurt readability. A misconception is thinking destructuring copies the object; it does not perform a deep clone — it merely binds selected references to new local variables. For state updates or copies, pair destructuring with the spread operator to create new objects instead of mutating existing ones. Destructuring objects — extract props with clarity means use destructuring to make props and api data extraction concise, while avoiding deep nested patterns that reduce readability.. In practical terms, unpack object properties into variables for cleaner component code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Destructuring Objects
Basic syntax
Unpack properties from objects into variables in one statement. You can also rename and set defaults.
// basic
const user = { name: 'Sam', age: 28 };
const { name, age } = user;

// rename and default
const { name: userName, email = 'unknown@example.com' } = user;
Key takeaway
Destructuring reduces boilerplate when extracting known properties and improves readability.
Nested destructuring & caution
You may destructure nested objects, but deep patterns can be fragile if the shape is inconsistent. Consider safe defaults or optional chaining before nesting patterns.
// nested
const response = { user: { id: 1, profile: { name: 'Lee' } } };
const { user: { profile: { name } = {} } = {} } = response;
Common mistake
Assuming destructuring performs safety checks. If a path is undefined you may get an error; use defaults or optional chaining when necessary.

screens.title: Destructuring arrays and the rest pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Array destructuring lets you assign elements to named variables in order, which is handy when functions return tuples or when you only need the first few items. You can also skip items and provide defaults. The rest operator, when used in array patterns, collects remaining elements into a fresh array. This is often used when you want the head and the tail of a list: take the first item and gather the rest for separate processing. A common use case in React Native is extracting the first item for a highlight and keeping the remaining items for a list. Be aware that array destructuring is position-based, not name-based, so you must know the index of items you want. Also remember rest in destructuring produces shallow copies of the remaining elements, not deep clones. Use rest for function parameters to accept a variable number of arguments and use array rest to partition data into head and tail cleanly. Destructuring arrays and the rest pattern means use array destructuring with rest to separate the first elements from the remaining list and to accept variable arguments in functions.. In practical terms, extract items and gather the remainder into a single array. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Head and tail
keyIdea.text: Use array destructuring with rest to separate the first elements from the remaining list and to accept variable arguments in functions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Array destructuring & rest
Array destructuring
Bind elements by position. Use defaults for missing items and skip positions with commas.
const arr = [10, 20, 30, 40];
const [first, second] = arr; // 10, 20
const [head, ...tail] = arr; // head=10, tail=[20,30,40]
const [a, , c = 0] = [1]; // a=1, c=0 (default)
Tip
Use rest to capture remaining items into a new array for non-destructive processing.
Function parameters with rest
Rest gathers a variable number of arguments into a real array you can iterate over.
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((s, n) => s + n, 0);
}

sum(1,2,3); // 6
Misconception
Rest is not the same as spread. Rest collects into a new array; spread expands elements into a context like a literal or function call.

screens.title: Spread operator for arrays and objects
screens.narratorSegment: The spread operator expands an iterable or object into individual elements. It is a lightweight way to copy arrays and objects or to merge them. For arrays, you often use spread to create a new array that appends or prepends items while preserving the original: this is crucial for React state updates where mutation can lead to subtle bugs. For objects, spread creates a shallow copy of enumerable properties and can be used to override or extend fields. A typical pattern merges base styles with overrides by creating a new object that spreads the base then spreads the override, so the override wins. Be mindful this is a shallow operation: nested objects remain referenced, so changing a nested field may still mutate original nested state. A common mistake is assuming spread produces a deep clone. When nested data requires immutability, compose shallow copies at each level or use helper utilities designed for deep updates. Spread is powerful, but pair it with the right level of copying for your data shape. Spread operator for arrays and objects means spread creates a shallow copy—great for top-level updates like merging styles or elements. for nested updates, create new copies at each level.. In practical terms, copy, merge, and extend data without mutating originals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Spread Operator
Array patterns
Create new arrays by spreading existing ones. This avoids mutating the original reference.
const oldArray = [1,2];
const newArray = [...oldArray, 3]; // [1,2,3]

// insert at front
const front = [0, ...oldArray];
Key takeaway
Use spread to produce new arrays and avoid in-place operations like push in state updates.
Object merge example
Combine base properties with overrides while creating a new object reference.
const base = {a:1, b:2};
const override = {b:20, c:3};
const merged = { ...base, ...override }; // {a:1,b:20,c:3}

const cardStyle = { ...baseStyle, backgroundColor: '#e0e0e0' };
Common mistake
Thinking spread does a deep clone. For nested objects, create new copies at each nested level instead of relying on a single spread.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Rest Operator
Function parameters
Gather arguments into an array parameter to accept variable inputs.
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

sum(1, 2, 3); // 6
Use case
Build flexible wrappers around APIs that accept varying numbers of arguments.
Object rest example
Extract named fields and collect the remainder into a new object for forwarding props or building reduced objects.
const person = { name: 'John', age: 30, city: 'NY' };
const { name, age, ...otherInfo } = person;
// otherInfo = { city: 'NY' }
Misconception
Rest is not spread. Rest collects into a new array or object. Spread expands elements into a literal or call.

screens.title: ES6 Modules: import and export patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Modules are the standard way to organize JavaScript into separate files that export values and import them where needed. Named exports allow multiple named bindings to be exported from one module and imported selectively with curly braces. Default export provides a single primary value from a file and is imported without braces. Use named exports for utility collections and default export for a single main component or function. Named exports allow multiple exports; default provides a single primary export.

export const PI = 3.14;

screens.title: Pitfalls, pro tips, and checks
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate common pitfalls and everyday pro tips so you can avoid regressions in React Native code. First, avoid using var in new code because hoisting and function scope can cause variables to be visible in unexpected places. Second, remember const does not freeze objects; to avoid accidental mutation, construct new objects with spread when updating state. fullNarratorScript:
Before we build interfaces in React Native, we need a reliable command of modern JavaScript. This lesson refreshes the core ES6 features you will use: block-scoped declarations, arrow functions, destructuring, the spread and rest operators, and ES6 modules. Each of these features reduces boilerplate and makes component code easier to reason about. For example, choosing a block-scoped declaration prevents accidental leakage of variables across loops and conditionals. Arrow functions keep your callbacks concise and avoid common mistakes with the this keyword in component methods. Destructuring and the spread operator let you pick only the values you need and produce immutable-looking updates without mutating originals. Finally, import and export let you organize logic into small, testable files used across screens and components. We will walk through practical examples, a guided refactor of a small component, and a short assessment that asks you to apply destructuring and rest. By the end you will know not just the syntax but the practical trade-offs and common pitfalls to avoid. Ready to make your JavaScript cleaner and safer for React Native?

By the end of these screens you will have clearly defined, demonstrable skills you can apply to React Native. First, you will differentiate var, let, and const, and explain block scope versus function scope with concrete examples that show why let and const are safer. Second, you will write arrow functions that use implicit return and understand lexical this, particularly when writing callbacks or handlers inside components. Third, you will destructure objects and arrays to extract values succinctly from props and A P I responses. Finally, you will combine spread and rest operators to copy, merge, and collect values without mutating originals. For each objective we pair a short practice mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can test yourself. These objectives are intentionally practical: you will refactor a small component to use const and arrow functions, apply destructuring to props, and use spread to merge styles. That work makes these objectives concrete, not abstract. As you study, look for how each feature reduces boilerplate and prevents specific bugs like accidental global variables, lost this context, or unintended object mutation.

This second objectives screen ties each skill to a practical task so you can check understanding as you go. You will refactor a small React Native component, replacing var with const and let and changing function declarations to arrow functions to remove binding problems. You will also extract props using destructuring and update style objects using the spread operator so you avoid mutating shared objects. In addition, you'll write a small utility file and use named and default exports to reuse code across components. Each objective is paired with a short practice action: run a small test that verifies a refactor or write a one-line arrow function that returns a value. These tasks train the habit of choosing const by default, using let only when reassigning, preferring destructuring for readability, and using modules to keep files small. With these practices you reduce common runtime errors and make your codebase easier to maintain as it scales.

Let's define the three main declaration keywords and compare their behavior with concrete examples. The older keyword is var, which is function-scoped and hoisted: a variable declared with var is visible throughout its containing function even before the declaration line runs. That behavior can lead to surprising bugs when variables appear to exist earlier than you expect. In contrast, let and const are block-scoped: their visibility is limited to the nearest pair of curly braces. That prevents accidental access from outside loops, conditionals, or nested blocks. The practical difference between let and const is reassignment. Use const for bindings that should not be reassigned; use let only when you need to update a variable. A common misconception is thinking const means an immutable object; actually it prevents reassigning the binding, but object properties or array elements can still be modified. For example, a constant array can have items pushed into it, but you cannot assign a new array to the same name. A good rule of thumb is to default to const and switch to let when you deliberately plan to reassign. This habit reduces accidental reassignments and clarifies intent in component code.

A small but important habit improves code safety: default to const. When you declare most variables with const, you communicate intent and reduce accidental reassignments. That habit makes refactors clearer because a later reader knows the binding is not meant to change. However, a common confusion is that const makes values immutable. In JavaScript, const prevents the name from being rebound to a new value, but if the value is an object or array its contents remain changeable. That means you can push into a constant array or set properties on a constant object. This distinction matters in React Native where state updates often require creating a new array or object rather than mutating an existing one. Use the spread operator to build new arrays or objects for state updates so you maintain immutable update patterns. In practice, prefer const for every binding that doesn't need reassignment, and be explicit about when you mutate an object — or better, avoid mutation and return a new copy. This approach reduces subtle bugs and makes your components easier to test. Using const effectively and mutability nuance means const signals intent not immutability. use spread patterns for state updates to avoid in-place mutation despite const bindings.. In practical terms, why default to const and how object mutation works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Arrow functions simplify function expressions and clarify how this behaves inside callbacks. They provide concise syntax: a single-expression arrow implicitly returns that value, eliminating the return keyword. More importantly, arrow functions do not create their own this binding. Instead they inherit the this value from the enclosing lexical context. This trait addresses common pitfalls when passing callbacks to event handlers or timers inside components. For example, if you use a traditional function for a timer callback inside a component method, the this inside that callback may not refer to the component instance unless you explicitly bind it. Arrow functions capture the surrounding this, preventing that need. A common misconception is that arrow functions are always interchangeable with regular functions; they are not, because they cannot be used as constructors and they lack their own prototype. When you need a function with its own this or a constructor, use a normal function. For typical React Native callbacks and render helpers, arrow functions are concise and reliable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Destructuring extracts properties from objects into local variables in a concise form. This is especially useful in React Native for pulling props from a component's props object or fields from A P I responses. Instead of assigning each property one by one, destructuring lets you declare the variables you need in a single pattern. You can also rename properties or provide default values when a property might be absent. A common use case is extracting name and email from a user object returned by an A P I, which reduces repetition and improves readability. Another helpful pattern is nested destructuring for objects that contain nested shapes, but use it sparingly when nested depths grow deep as it can hurt readability. A misconception is thinking destructuring copies the object; it does not perform a deep clone — it merely binds selected references to new local variables. For state updates or copies, pair destructuring with the spread operator to create new objects instead of mutating existing ones. Destructuring objects — extract props with clarity means use destructuring to make props and api data extraction concise, while avoiding deep nested patterns that reduce readability.. In practical terms, unpack object properties into variables for cleaner component code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Array destructuring lets you assign elements to named variables in order, which is handy when functions return tuples or when you only need the first few items. You can also skip items and provide defaults. The rest operator, when used in array patterns, collects remaining elements into a fresh array. This is often used when you want the head and the tail of a list: take the first item and gather the rest for separate processing. A common use case in React Native is extracting the first item for a highlight and keeping the remaining items for a list. Be aware that array destructuring is position-based, not name-based, so you must know the index of items you want. Also remember rest in destructuring produces shallow copies of the remaining elements, not deep clones. Use rest for function parameters to accept a variable number of arguments and use array rest to partition data into head and tail cleanly. In practical terms, extract items and gather the remainder into a single array. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The spread operator expands an iterable or object into individual elements. It is a lightweight way to copy arrays and objects or to merge them. For arrays, you often use spread to create a new array that appends or prepends items while preserving the original: this is crucial for React state updates where mutation can lead to subtle bugs. For objects, spread creates a shallow copy of enumerable properties and can be used to override or extend fields. A typical pattern merges base styles with overrides by creating a new object that spreads the base then spreads the override, so the override wins. Be mindful this is a shallow operation: nested objects remain referenced, so changing a nested field may still mutate original nested state. A common mistake is assuming spread produces a deep clone. When nested data requires immutability, compose shallow copies at each level or use helper utilities designed for deep updates. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In function parameters, rest gathers any number of trailing arguments into an array that you can iterate or reduce. Modules are the standard way to organize JavaScript into separate files that export values and import them where needed. Named exports allow multiple named bindings to be exported from one module and imported selectively with curly braces. Default export provides a single primary value from a file and is imported without braces. Use named exports for utility collections and default export for a single main component or function. In React Native, exporting components and utilities from small files keeps screens compact and encourages reuse. A common pitfall is mixing default and named exports incorrectly: importing a named export without braces or a default export with braces will fail. Another good practice is to keep exports small and focused — export small, testable functions rather than large monolithic modules. This pattern makes it straightforward to mock or stub dependencies in tests and to reason about data flow across components. Let's consolidate common pitfalls and everyday pro tips so you can avoid regressions in React Native code. First, avoid using var in new code because hoisting and function scope can cause variables to be visible in unexpected places. Second, remember const does not freeze objects; to avoid accidental mutation, construct new objects with spread when updating state. Third, arrow functions are concise but not suitable where a constructor or separate this binding is required. Fourth, be careful with shallow copies: the spread operator creates shallow clones, so nested objects remain shared — when you need deep updates, create new copies at each nested level. Fifth, destructuring is great for clarity, but nested destructuring can become fragile if the data shape is unpredictable — prefer explicit checks or defaults. Let's summarize three essential concepts from this chapter so you can recall them quickly as you code. First, let and const are block-scoped and generally safer than var due to predictable scoping. Default to const and use let only when you need reassignment. Second, arrow functions provide concise syntax and capture the lexical this, which avoids manual binding in most component callbacks. They are not appropriate for constructors or when you need a function with its own this. Third, destructuring assignment gives you a compact way to extract properties from objects and items from arrays, improving readability when dealing with props or A P I responses. Pair destructuring with default values to avoid runtime errors when fields are missing. Keep these three ideas in mind when writing or refactoring React Native components to reduce boilerplate and common bugs.

Finish with three more practical reminders that reinforce correct patterns. First, the spread operator creates shallow copies of arrays and objects and is the go-to pattern for merging or extending top-level data without mutating originals. Second, the rest operator collects variable arguments into an array or remaining properties into an object, which is useful for flexible function APIs and partitioning data. Third, use ES6 modules to structure small, focused files with named exports for utilities and default exports for primary components. Together these patterns enable small, testable code units and predictable state updates. As a quick habit, run small tests after refactors, verify that references change when you expect a new object, and prefer shallow copies at each level for nested updates.
